pull.title: crypto: plug hardware optimized SHA256 into libsecp256k1's context
pull.body:
Since https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/pull//1777 , libsecp256k1 allows an externally provided SHA256 compression function. This PR plug ours in, so it runs on our SHA-NI/ARMv8/SSE4 hardware optimized implementation instead of the libsecp bare internal one.

The biggest gains are at the signing side, not at the verification side.

The first commits restructure how the libsecp context is encapsulated and initialized. `ECC_Context` now properly handles the libsecp context lifecycle and fully behaves as a singleton, getting decoupled from the `key.h/cpp` primitive (which is no longer accessed by upper layers just to init ECC), allowing us to introduce a verification context within the same object, and moving the singleton initialization to `ecc_init.h` which simplifies usage to a single entry point for all users.

Benchmarks at the bench introduction commit (43c9bdbf8ada1b581b5ab1f0a102517c243a60da) and at the tip:

On ARM64, `arm_shani` implementation

| benchmark | before | after | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ECDSASign` | 79.2 µs | 69.3 µs | -13% |
| `SchnorrSign` | 39.9 µs | 37.1 µs | -7% |
| `ECDSAVerify` | 27.4 µs | 27.3 µs | -0% |
| `SchnorrVerify` | 28.1 µs | 27.8 µs | -1% |
| `EllSwiftCreate` | 29.8 µs | 28.8 µs | -3% |
| `BIP324_ECDH` | 30.4 µs | 30.1 µs | -1% |

events.body:
tACK ecf779fa06cef78ca668715cba21b30a1fda8a06

On an Apple M5 (arm_shani), a differential harness compared a context using libsecp256k1's own compression with one using `SHA256Transform`, with both Core's arm_shani and portable transforms. It ran 20,000 random rounds of tagged hashes, BIP340 signing of 0- to 300-byte messages, ECDSA, ElligatorSwift XDH, MuSig2 and silent payments labels, plus the BIP340 vectors. All results matched, and a sample also matched the pure-Python code of a library I maintain. Unit tests and ctest pass.

Medians of three interleaved bench_bitcoin runs against 7caaaca9d2, the commit before the plug: ECDSASign -11%, SchnorrSign -3.7%, EllSwiftCreate -3.7%, BIP324_ECDH -1.9%, SchnorrVerify -1.2%. The ConnectBlock benches stay within noise. With Core's portable transform forced, hashing and signing run at libsecp256k1's own speed, so a CPU that falls back to it loses nothing per operation.

Non-blocking: ECCContextCreate goes from 13.5 µs to 176 µs. Almost all of it is the libsecp256k1 self-test of the plugged function, run once for each of the two contexts: 88 µs each here, about 0.5 ms each with the portable transform. Creating the verify context with `secp256k1_context_clone` before randomizing the sign context keeps the plugged function and skips the second test. From reading the code, not measuring, this matters mainly for the `secp256k1_ecdsa_signature_parse_der_lax` fuzz target, which builds a context for every input that parses. Happy to share the scripts as a gist.
@theStack can you take another look here?

author furszy <matiasfurszyfer@protonmail.com> 1788807011 -0400
committer furszy <matiasfurszyfer@protonmail.com> 1793633889 -0500

libsecp: introduce public verification context

Verification uses secp256k1_context_static, which can't take our
optimized SHA256 compression function. Rather than reusing the signing
context, which blinds certain calculations, for no benefit to public
data, verification gets its own context, owned by ECC_Context along
with the signing one.

Around 1% faster Schnorr signature verification. ECDSA remains equal
as hashing is done outside libsecp.

events.body:
Updated per @theStack feedback. Thanks!
Applied the `GetSecp256k1PublicContext` renaming and the functions' doc improvement. Left the `GetSecp256k1SecretContext` one for a quick scripted-diff as otherwise it requires a rework of this branch from the second commit onwards.

comments.body: minimal-diff nit: from all the secp function calls in this file, this (`_schnorrsig_verify`) is the only one that involves hashing and thus benefits from the SHA256 override, i.e. it would be fine if the others kept using the static context

An alternative to this split-up would be to keep having only one "full" (i.e. non-static) context and use it for both signing and verifying (and any other API calls that either involve a generator point multiplication or  hashing). It's true that some functions don't take use of the blinding data generated with `_context_randomize`, but it also doesn't slow things down or hurt in another way.
The only challenge might be to find a good name for that context, since it's not only used for signing anymore (`FullContext`, `DynamicContext`, ...?).

> An alternative to this split-up would be to keep having only one "full" (i.e. non-static) context and use it for both signing and verifying (and any other API calls that either involve a generator point multiplication or hashing). It's true that some functions don't take use of the blinding data generated with _context_randomize, but it also doesn't slow things down or hurt in another way.

What if we ever want to re-seed the context rng? (`secp256k1_context_randomize` docs suggests doing it). By having two contexts, we avoid adding a mutex on the verification side and keep that context immutable and thread safe after construction.

> > An alternative to this split-up would be to keep having only one "full" (i.e. non-static) context and use it for both signing and verifying (and any other API calls that either involve a generator point multiplication or hashing). It's true that some functions don't take use of the blinding data generated with _context_randomize, but it also doesn't slow things down or hurt in another way.
> 
> What if we ever want to re-seed the context rng? (`secp256k1_context_randomize` docs suggests doing it). By having two contexts, we avoid adding a mutex on the verification side and keep that context immutable and thread safe after construction.

Fair point, I didn't consider that there could be potential use-cases where the context needs any further modification after its initial setup in `ECC_Start`. Not sure how realistic plans of implementing re-seeding in Core currently are (and what the actual gain in security would really be by doing that), but I agree it's worth to take into account. No strong objection on the split-up, but wanted to bring the simpler option for discussion.

> Not sure how realistic plans of implementing re-seeding in Core currently are (and what the actual gain in security would really be by doing that),

I suspect there's a real gain when it comes to certain types of side-channel attack (e.g., power analysis). There were many discussions in the past, and I wrote [a libsecp256k1 issue](https://github.com/bitcoin-core/secp256k1/issues/1141) a while ago. The problem is just that nobody is working on it. ;)

The simplest thing we could do is to re-randomize the context after every operation that makes an ecmult_gen (pubkey generation and signing). This would be a ~100% hit in performance for these operations because rerandomizing also needs an ecmult_gen. 100% sounds huge but I'm not sure if anyone would really care here for these operations.

If people do care, the next simplest thing is to it only after (every n operations). For example, if we set n=10, then the performance hit is only 10%.

Anyway, this discussion belongs to a separate issue. But I agree that it's worth taking into account.

Nice issue write-up. 

I think we shouldn't over-think this now. Most of the work in this PR is about structuring the code properly so that we don't continue expanding the technical debt (the transform callback plug could have been done in 2 commits max otherwise, but they would be built on top of a dirty base). Once this lands, any future decision should be simple to do and isolated.

We can actually drop the ECC context creation  from the `parse_der_lax` fuzz target, nothing there requires it.
Other than that, the concept of the change seems good to me, the only thing I would try to do is decoupling the ECC function calls out of the `ECC_Context` constructor, so it stays clean.

This call appears redundant. Both `bitcoind.cpp` and `NodeImpl::baseInitialize()` construct a `kernel::Context`, which already runs `SHA256AutoDetect()` before ECC initialization.

> This call appears redundant.

Not for benchmarks, unit and fuzz tests. It doesn't harm to keep it.

`bench_bitcoin` already calls it in `main()` at ecf779fa06, and tests using `BasicTestingSetup` initialize it through `kernel::Context`.
It is redundant for those callers, although the extra overhead is negligible during normal startup.
